# Online Shopping System Advanced — how to build it

You have two folders. This is what to do with them.

| Folder | Use it for |
|---|---|
| [`01-scope-spec/`](01-scope-spec/) | **What** to build and when it is done. Requirements, features, acceptance gates. |
| [`02-tech-spec/`](02-tech-spec/) | **How** to build it. Data, flows, interfaces, threats, tests. |

**Give a developer or a coding agent both.** The technical folder alone produces something that works and cannot be signed off, because nothing in it says what *done* means. The scope folder alone cannot be built from. Neither half is optional.

---

## Before the first line of code

| # | Do this | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read [`01-scope-spec/SCOPE-SPEC.md`](01-scope-spec/SCOPE-SPEC.md), then [`02-tech-spec/TECH-SPEC.md`](02-tech-spec/TECH-SPEC.md). Half an hour. | You cannot judge a plan for work you have not read the scope of. |
| 2 | Resolve every `DECISION REQUIRED`. | An assumed answer becomes rework the week before release. |
| 3 | Work down `PLACEHOLDERS.md`. | Each is a value the specification needs and does not have. A `{{PLACEHOLDER}}` reaching review is a review failure. |
| 4 | Write the context file — `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` — at the repository root: build, test and lint commands with their healthy output, the conventions, and the mistakes agents keep making here. | It is the single highest-return file in the repository, and it is what makes an agent's output consistent with yours. |
| 5 | Name one command that decides whether a change is correct, and state it as the definition of done. | *It works on my machine* is not a gate. |

## Then build one capability at a time

Not layer by layer. A horizontal slice — all the models, then all the endpoints — means nothing works until the end, so nothing is verifiable until the end.

|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **administration** | [`02-tech-spec/administration/TECH-SPEC.md`](02-tech-spec/administration/TECH-SPEC.md) | every `GATE-` in [`01-scope-spec/administration/SCOPE-SPEC.md`](01-scope-spec/administration/SCOPE-SPEC.md) holds with its evidence |
| 2 | **audit-trail** | [`02-tech-spec/audit-trail/TECH-SPEC.md`](02-tech-spec/audit-trail/TECH-SPEC.md) | every `GATE-` in [`01-scope-spec/audit-trail/SCOPE-SPEC.md`](01-scope-spec/audit-trail/SCOPE-SPEC.md) holds with its evidence |
| 3 | **authentication** | [`02-tech-spec/authentication/TECH-SPEC.md`](02-tech-spec/authentication/TECH-SPEC.md) | every `GATE-` in [`01-scope-spec/authentication/SCOPE-SPEC.md`](01-scope-spec/authentication/SCOPE-SPEC.md) holds with its evidence |
| 4 | **authentication-sessions** | [`02-tech-spec/authentication-sessions/TECH-SPEC.md`](02-tech-spec/authentication-sessions/TECH-SPEC.md) | every `GATE-` in [`01-scope-spec/authentication-sessions/SCOPE-SPEC.md`](01-scope-spec/authentication-sessions/SCOPE-SPEC.md) holds with its evidence |
| 5 | **authentication-signup** | [`02-tech-spec/authentication-signup/TECH-SPEC.md`](02-tech-spec/authentication-signup/TECH-SPEC.md) | every `GATE-` in [`01-scope-spec/authentication-signup/SCOPE-SPEC.md`](01-scope-spec/authentication-signup/SCOPE-SPEC.md) holds with its evidence |
| 6 | **authorisation** | [`02-tech-spec/authorisation/TECH-SPEC.md`](02-tech-spec/authorisation/TECH-SPEC.md) | every `GATE-` in [`01-scope-spec/authorisation/SCOPE-SPEC.md`](01-scope-spec/authorisation/SCOPE-SPEC.md) holds with its evidence |
| 7 | **payments** | [`02-tech-spec/payments/TECH-SPEC.md`](02-tech-spec/payments/TECH-SPEC.md) | every `GATE-` in [`01-scope-spec/payments/SCOPE-SPEC.md`](01-scope-spec/payments/SCOPE-SPEC.md) holds with its evidence |
| 8 | **search** | [`02-tech-spec/search/TECH-SPEC.md`](02-tech-spec/search/TECH-SPEC.md) | every `GATE-` in [`01-scope-spec/search/SCOPE-SPEC.md`](01-scope-spec/search/SCOPE-SPEC.md) holds with its evidence |

Order them by dependency, not by importance: identity before anything that needs a subject, the data model before the flows that read it. The most important capability is rarely the first buildable one.

### The loop, per capability

1. **Read both halves of the capability** — its scope file and its tech file.
2. **Plan the slice** and have somebody read the plan. This is the cheapest place to catch a design error.
3. **Commit the plan on a clean tree.** That commit is where you return to if the slice goes wrong.
4. **Build it**, then run the verification command before telling anyone it is done.
5. **Write the tests the specification already named** — each `TEST-` row, citing its `REQ-` identifier in the test name.
6. **Commit, citing the requirements satisfied.** Six months later this is the only thing that answers *when did this start working*.
7. **Move the gate.** `PASS` only with the evidence attached; a gate nobody moved reads `NOT EVALUATED`, and that at release time is a discovery rather than a status.

## Adding a feature later

This is where a specification usually starts lying. The rule that prevents it is one sentence:

> **The specification changes first, in its own commit, before the code.**

Not because it is tidier. Because the order is the only part a reviewer can see — change both together and nobody can tell whether the code drifted or the contract moved.

| The request is | Do this |
|---|---|
| **A defect** — the code does not do what the specification says | Write a failing test citing the requirement it breaches, then fix the code. The specification does not change. |
| **A specification defect** — the code matches a specification that is wrong | Amend the requirement, its tests and its gate. Commit that alone. *Then* change the code. |
| **New work** — nobody specified this | It re-enters at the beginning: describe it, regenerate the specification with the new capability, and take the new slice through the loop above. |

### Regenerating without breaking what exists

The builder keeps every specification it has generated. Open the one you started from, add the new capability or change an answer, and generate a new **version** — the previous one is kept and the two can be compared side by side.

Because every identifier is scoped to its capability — `REQ-LOGIN-01`, `REQ-BILLING-01` — adding a capability cannot renumber an existing one. New requirements arrive with new identifiers; the ones you have already built and signed off keep theirs. That is what makes an amendment additive rather than a rewrite.

| What you changed | What happens to existing work |
|---|---|
| Added a capability | Nothing existing changes. A new folder appears in both halves, with its own identifiers. |
| Answered an outstanding decision | The `DECISION REQUIRED` becomes a register entry. Any requirement already built against it is unaffected. |
| Changed an answer to a question | Only that capability's content moves. The profile record lists what changed and why. |
| Changed the rigor tier or the architecture | More documents appear, or fewer. Existing requirement identifiers are unchanged; the profile says what was added or dropped, and why. |

Compare the new version against the old before you act on it. What matters is not the size of the diff but whether anything you have already accepted has moved.
